title: Friction

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Laws of Motion

summary: Friction is the opposing force at contact surfaces; static friction (up to a maximum) prevents motion from starting, kinetic friction acts once sliding occurs and is generally smaller than the maximum static value.
explanation: Friction arises from microscopic irregularities and molecular attraction between two surfaces in contact, opposing relative sliding or the tendency to slide. Static friction fs adjusts itself (self-regulating) to exactly balance the applied force up to a maximum value fs(max) = μsN, where μs is the coefficient of static friction and N is the normal reaction; beyond this the object starts to slide. Once sliding, kinetic friction fk = μkN opposes the relative motion, and experimentally μk < μs for most surface pairs, which is why it takes more force to start moving an object than to keep it moving. Rolling friction (relevant to wheels/balls) is much smaller than sliding friction because deformation at the contact patch, not sliding, dominates — this is why wheels are more efficient than dragging. The angle of friction (tanλ = μs) is the angle the resultant of normal force and limiting friction makes with the normal, and equals the angle of repose — the maximum incline angle at which a body remains at rest without sliding.
commonMisconceptions: Treating friction as a fixed force regardless of the applied force — static friction is variable and only reaches μsN at the verge of sliding.

Assuming kinetic friction depends on the contact area or the speed of sliding — to a good approximation it depends only on the normal force and the materials in contact (Coulomb's laws of friction), not on visible contact area.
Confusing angle of friction with angle of repose — they are numerically equal but describe different physical setups (friction triangle vs. an object resting on an incline).
examples: A block on a table needs a bigger push to start moving than to keep moving at constant velocity, because μs > μk.
Ball bearings replace sliding friction with much smaller rolling friction to reduce energy loss in machines.
genZNote: Static friction really said 'I match your energy' — right up until it can't anymore.
